extracted.intended_audience: General readers, law students, and practitioners interested in U.S. patent law—particularly willful infringement and enhanced damages
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the legal standards and guidance for finding willful patent infringement and awarding enhanced damages following Halo Electronics v. Pulse, including statutory text, prior Federal Circuit tests, and Supreme Court and concurring guidance. Useful for understanding when enhanced damages may be available and limits on proof and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhanced damages under 35 U.S.C. § 284
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory text: if a defendant is found to infringe, 'the court may increase the damages up to three times the amount found or assessed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court treated §284 as a broad, discretionary grant of authority to increase damages (up to treble). Halo held that this broad standard is incompatible with the Federal Circuit's narrower Seagate test and that courts have discretion to award enhanced damages based on egregious conduct, without being constrained by Seagate's specific requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seagate test (pre-Halo two-part test for willfulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit's two-part Seagate test required (1) an 'objective' showing that the infringement was objectively reckless and (2) a 'subjective' showing of the defendant's state of mind; it also required proof by 'clear and convincing evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court overruled Seagate in Halo, criticizing the test as inconsistent with §284 because it was unduly rigid, incentivized defendants to manufacture defenses to appear reasonable, and imposed procedural requirements (objective-recklessness and heightened burden of proof) not found in the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective-recklessness requirement (Seagate objective prong)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seagate required that willful infringement be shown only when a defendant acted in an 'objectively reckless' manner in infringing a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halo found this objective-recklessness requirement incompatible with §284's broad discretion. The Court warned that Seagate's objective-prong could encourage fabricating defenses and thus incorrectly shield some actionable conduct from enhanced damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear-and-convincing burden for willfulness (Seagate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Seagate, a finding of willfulness required 'clear and convincing evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court in Halo criticized imposing a heightened evidentiary standard not present in §284 and indicated that Seagate's 'clear and convincing' requirement was improper. Halo directed courts to apply the statute's discretionary standard rather than Seagate's heightened proof rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference in appellate standard of review for willfulness findings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court directed the Federal Circuit to adopt a more deferential standard of review toward district court findings of willfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halo emphasized that district courts are best positioned to determine whether conduct is sufficiently egregious to warrant enhanced damages and that appellate review should respect those factual determinations rather than substitute de novo review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willfulness requires more than mere knowledge of the patent (Breyer concurrence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice Breyer (concurring), joined by Kennedy and Alito, observed that evidence showing only knowledge of a patent would likely not meet the standard for willful infringement; rather, willfulness would require both knowledge of the patent and additional evidence of egregious conduct by the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breyer stressed that findings of willfulness should be reserved for 'egregious misconduct.' This concurrence narrows practical application by indicating that mere awareness of a patent does not suffice to justify enhanced damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: §298 restriction on use of advice-of-counsel (evidence of not obtaining counsel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 298 of the Patent Act prevents a fact-finder from considering evidence that a defendant failed to obtain the advice of counsel prior to infringing the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The concurrence highlights that lack of advice-of-counsel evidence should not be used against defendants when assessing willfulness; courts must not consider absence of counsel as proof of culpability under §298.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on using enhanced damages to recompense litigation costs (relation to §285)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice Breyer noted that any damages awarded for willful infringement should not be used to compensate a plaintiff for the cost of bringing suit, because those costs are already subject to being awarded under §285 of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enhanced damages under §284 are meant to punish/deter egregious infringing behavior, not to duplicate fee-shifting or compensate for litigation expenses; courts should avoid double recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-Halo treatment of a defendant's reasonable belief in invalidity as a defense to willfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Seagate-era decisions, a defendant's reasonable belief that a patent was invalid could preclude a finding of willfulness (district court and Federal Circuit concluded Pulse's belief in invalidity precluded willfulness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halo criticized Seagate's structure that effectively insulated defendants who could advance (even weakly grounded) reasonable-looking defenses; after Halo, a reasonable belief of invalidity remains relevant as factual evidence but does not automatically bar enhanced damages under the statute's broader standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Halo uncertainty and concern about when willfulness is warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentators reacted that eliminating Seagate produced mixed results: some praised removing an artificially restrictive test, while others worried about the lack of clear guidance and inconsistent subsequent decisions on when willfulness findings are appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should expect continued case-by-case development; Halo grants district courts discretion to punish egregious misconduct but leaves open questions about the precise boundary of conduct warranting enhanced damages, resulting in variable post-Halo jurisprudence.
